content: If you experience any of the following signs that a seizure is occurring or may occur, you should seek medical attention immediately. These signs include muscle twitching, jerking, spasms, tremors, or other uncontrolled movements. You may also notice stiffening of your arms and legs, feelings of anxiety, nervousness, confusion, or a sense of dread. Other symptoms include dizziness, lightheadedness, falling, or losing consciousness. Kidney damage is a potential risk when using oxacillin. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience symptoms such as a reduced need to urinate, swelling in your feet, ankles, or legs, unusual weakness or fatigue, difficulty breathing, chest pain or pressure, confusion, nausea, or seizures. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea can occur due to an overgrowth of bacteria called Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) in your gut, which may happen with many antibiotics, including oxacillin. This condition can develop even up to two months after stopping the antibiotic. Symptoms to watch for include watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea that does not resolve, blood in your stool, severe stomach cramps, or fever that begins after starting or finishing the medication. If you experience any of these symptoms, contact your healthcare provider immediately. Oxacillin can cause blood disorders, such as eosinophilia, agranulocytosis, neutropenia, and bone marrow suppression. Stop using oxacillin and seek medical help immediately if you experience symptoms such as fever, shortness of breath, pale or yellowish skin, easy bruising or bleeding, frequent infections, unusual weakness or fatigue, dizziness, lightheadedness, fainting, headache, or a fast or abnormal heartbeat. Liver damage, also known as hepatotoxicity, is another potential risk of oxacillin use. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, stomach or abdominal pain, fever, unusual weakness or fatigue, itching, loss of appetite, light-colored stool, dark-colored urine, or yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes (jaundice). People who are allergic to oxacillin or any of its ingredients should not use this medication. If you are unsure about the ingredients in your specific oxacillin product, consult your pharmacist. Additionally, oxacillin is typically administered by a healthcare provider in a hospital or clinic setting. If you store oxacillin at home, do not share it with others, even if they have the same condition, as it may harm them. Keep oxacillin out of reach of children. Before using oxacillin, inform your healthcare provider about all your health conditions and any prescription or over-the-counter medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, or supplements you are taking. This information will help your provider determine if oxacillin is appropriate for you. Be sure to mention any allergies to penicillin, other medications, corn, or corn products, as well as any history of asthma, liver problems, kidney problems, or antibiotic-associated diarrhea. Oxacillin may interact with other medications and supplements. Inform your healthcare provider if you are using any tetracycline antibiotics (e.g., tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline, omadacycline, sarecycline) or probenecid, a medication commonly used for gout. This may not be a complete list of potential drug interactions, so always disclose all medications and supplements you are taking. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, inform your healthcare provider, as it is not known how oxacillin may affect pregnancy or an unborn baby. Your provider will advise you on whether you should use oxacillin during pregnancy. Similarly, if you are breastfeeding or planning to breastfeed, let your provider know, as oxacillin passes into breast milk. There are no known interactions between oxacillin and foods or drinks. However, it is unclear if alcohol consumption affects oxacillin. Heavy drinking can weaken your immune response and make it harder for your body to fight infections. If you accidentally use too much oxacillin, seek medical help immediately by calling 911 or contacting a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take only the next scheduled dose. Do not take double or extra doses. It is important to complete the full prescribed course of oxacillin, even if your symptoms improve, to reduce the risk of future infections becoming resistant to oxacillin or similar medications. The most common side effects of oxacillin include pain, swelling, or inflammation at the injection site, as well as rash. If these side effects bother you, inform your healthcare provider. There may be other side effects not listed here, so contact your provider if you suspect you are experiencing a side effect. Serious side effects of oxacillin, while less common, include severe allergic reactions. Stop using oxacillin and seek immediate medical attention if you experience symptoms such as breathing problems, wheezing, a racing heart, fever, general ill feeling, swollen lymph nodes, swelling of the face, lips, mouth, tongue, or throat, trouble swallowing, throat tightness, itching, skin rash, hives, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, lightheadedness, fainting, stomach cramps, or joint pain. Some individuals using oxacillin have reported seizures. Seizures can present in various forms, some of which may not be easily recognizable. Stop using oxacillin and contact your healthcare provider if you notice signs of a seizure, such as muscle twitching, jerking, spasms, tremors, or other uncontrolled movements, stiffening of the arms and legs, feelings of anxiety, nervousness, confusion, or dread, dizziness, lightheadedness, falling, or loss of consciousness.
